2.text: as the eagle and the raven. To kill the former would bring a dense fog.

3.text: In times of want, meat of foxes and wolves is often eaten, and the popular

4.text: saying for a man born of a poor family is that he has been raised on fox-meat.¹

5.text: VEGETABLE FOOD. — Vegetable food of various kinds is used by both

6.text: branches of the tribe, though rather as a substitute in cases of scarcity of

7.text: meat than as a relished change.

8.text: I have already mentioned the moss extracted from the paunch of the

9.text: reindeer. It is a soft greenish mass of the consistency of thick gruel. The

10.text: women strain it through a piece of old net. The coarse shreds of moss that

11.text: remain in the strainer are placed back in the paunch, and smoked for a long

12.text: time over the hearth. This method of preparation, however, is used princi-

13.text: pally by the Tungus. The Chukchee throw away the shreds and keep the

14.text: green gruel, which they use for preparing a soup by boiling it with some

15.text: blood, fat, and chopped guts of reindeer. In former times this soup formed

16.text: the usual breakfast of the Reindeer people. The moss-gruel was stored in

17.text: great quantities and used throughout the summer, but at present tea is gradually

19.text: Poor people still store a couple of bags for winter use every year, but

20.text: the greater part is left unused. In the fall, when the Chukchee have their

21.text: great slaughtering, the poor fishing-people of the Russian and Yakut settle-

22.text: ments of the Kolyma take some of it for dog-food without pay. With it

23.text: they thicken the fish-soup prepared for the dogs.

24.text: Leaves of stunted willows are gathered early in summer, pounded into

25.text: a pulp, mixed with moss-gruel, and put into bags, in which the mixture is

26.text: allowed to ferment. After fermentation it tastes sour, and is eaten with putrid

27.text: meat, like a salad, though not in large quantities.

28.text: Leaves of Polygonum polymorphum, Oxyria digina, Claytonia acutifolia

29.text: Willd, and several other plants, are used for the same purpose, or are eaten

30.text: raw, mixed with blood or putrid liver, or some animal food of similar kind.

31.text: The Maritime Chukchee pound these leaves and store them for winter use,

32.text: without admixture of moss-gruel. They eat also several kinds of seaweed

33.text: which are found on the seashore. This is gathered only when animal food

34.text: is scarce, but children eat it raw while playing on the beach.

35.text: The inner bark of the thickest roots of stunted willow is also utilized as

36.text: food. In olden times it was much more important than at present, as may

37.text: be judged from an ancient saying: “The people come to life in spring because

38.text: the roots of the willow begin to thaw.” The bark is stripped off, thoroughly

39.text: pounded, and then mixed with fresh or putrid blood, and eaten raw or boiled

40.text: as a kind of soup. The women also put some of this bark into the ferment-

41.text: ing blood, which is stored for winter use.
